title: JWT Pitfalls and Token Storage
description: Learn how JSON Web Tokens work, where they fail, and how to store them safely in browsers. Cover algorithm confusion attacks, token revocation, and the trade-offs between localStorage and httpOnly cookies.

data.text: JSON Web Tokens, or JWTs, are compact, URL-safe tokens that carry claims about a user. They are widely used in modern authentication because they are stateless: the server does not need to store session data, it simply verifies the token's signature and reads the claims. However, JWTs come with significant pitfalls that developers frequently overlook — poor storage, no built-in revocation, and algorithm confusion attacks are just the beginning.

A JWT has three parts separated by dots: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header declares the token type and signing algorithm. The payload contains claims — statements about the user like their ID, roles, and expiration time. The signature ensures the token was not tampered with. If an attacker can change the algorithm or remove the signature, they can forge tokens.

terms.definition: A compact, signed token consisting of header, payload, and signature parts.
Statements about a subject (user) encoded in the JWT payload, such as sub, email, and roles.
An attack where the token's algorithm is changed from asymmetric (RS256) to symmetric (HS256), allowing forgery with the public key.

data.title: JWT header and payload
data.content: A decoded JWT shows the algorithm in the header and claims in the payload.

data.title: Algorithm confusion is real
data.text: If your server accepts both RS256 and HS256, and an attacker knows your public RSA key, they can re-sign the token with HMAC-SHA256 using that public key as the secret. Always lock the algorithm to the expected value and never trust the token's alg header blindly.

Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens and System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt provide robust JWT validation in .NET. Always specify the exact signing algorithm, validate the issuer and audience, and enforce an expiration. Never accept tokens with `alg: none` — some older libraries would skip signature validation entirely if the header said none.

data.title: JWT validation with Microsoft.IdentityModel
data.content: Configure token validation parameters to lock the algorithm, issuer, and audience.

data.text: Where you store the token in the browser matters enormously. **localStorage** is easy to access from JavaScript but is vulnerable to XSS — any injected script can read every token. **httpOnly cookies** cannot be read by JavaScript, which blocks XSS token theft, but are vulnerable to CSRF unless protected with SameSite and anti-forgery tokens. For most web applications, httpOnly cookies with SameSite=Lax and short-lived access tokens are the safest default.

cards.title: localStorage
cards.description: Tokens stored in the browser's localStorage API. Accessible by any JavaScript on the page.

cards.title: httpOnly cookie
cards.description: Token stored in a cookie with the httpOnly flag, inaccessible to JavaScript.

cards.title: In-memory variable
cards.description: Token stored only in JavaScript memory and lost on page refresh.
pros: Survives XSS only while page is loaded
cons: Lost on refresh (requires re-login or refresh token)
Still vulnerable to XSS while page is open

data.text: Because JWTs are stateless, the server cannot revoke them without maintaining a blocklist — which defeats the stateless advantage. The practical solution is to keep access tokens very short-lived (5-15 minutes) and use refresh tokens with rotation. When a refresh token is used, the server issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If a token is leaked, the window of exposure is limited.

items.text: Lock the signing algorithm to RS256 or another explicit value.
items.hint: Reject tokens that specify a different algorithm or none at all.

items.text: Prefer httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies over localStorage for web apps.
items.hint: Cookies protect against XSS token theft, especially when combined with CSP.
Short lifetimes limit the window for token replay or theft.

items.text: Use refresh token rotation with a server-side blocklist for reuse detection.
items.hint: If a refresh token is presented twice, revoke the entire token family.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: JWTs carry signed claims but have no built-in revocation mechanism.
Algorithm confusion lets attackers forge tokens if the server accepts multiple algorithms.
httpOnly cookies are safer than localStorage for browser token storage.
Short-lived access tokens plus refresh token rotation limit the impact of token theft.
data.takeaway: Treat JWTs like passwords: store them safely, validate everything, and limit their lifetime.
